title: Why the village fed a hill
hookLine: a boy asks his father why they're cooking for Indra, and the whole village turns its offering to the hill
carry: God is in the hill that feeds you

cards: The whole village is cooking. Rice, sweets, milk dishes. The elders are busy getting ready for a sacrifice.
Krishna, a boy now, already knows the answer, the text says, but he goes to his father anyway and asks. Father, what's all this for? Who is it for?
What do we get from it? Nanda is patient with him. It's for Indra, he says, the king of the gods, the lord of the rain clouds.

teach.h: INDRA SENDS RAIN; WE HONOR HIM.
teach.b: Indra sends the rain, Nanda explains.

teach.h: WE LIVE BY FORESTS, HILLS, AND COWS.
teach.b: The rain grows the grass, the grass feeds the cows, and the cows feed us. So we honor him. Krishna answers with a different picture.
Beings are born and die by their own actions, he says. And what do we cowherds live by? Forests and hills.
So let's offer to what is right in front of us: the cows, the brahmins, and the hill, Govardhan, which shelters us and our herds. Cook everything you were going to cook.
Feed everyone, even the dogs, even the people at the edges of the village. Decorate the cattle, and walk around the hill. Nanda and the elders agree.
Then comes a strange and lovely detail.

As the people offer their food, Krishna takes on a vast new form, declares, I am the hill, and that great form eats the offerings, while the boy Krishna stands among the cowherds, bowing to it with them.

teach.h: GOVARDHAN PUJA: A MOUNTAIN OF FOOD.
teach.b: That's the first Govardhan Puja. In the days around Diwali, many Hindu families and temples still keep it.

They heap up an Annakut, a mountain of food, offer it to Krishna as the hill, and share it with everyone who comes. Pilgrims walk all the way around the real Govardhan, near Vrindavan, a walk of many miles.
The teaching: God isn't only far off, sending rain. He's in the hill, the cows, the people you feed. Somewhere up in the sky, Indra has noticed what's missing.

how: Some Hindu communities keep Govardhan Puja, in the days of Diwali, by building a small hill of food, called Annakut, and offering it, and pilgrims walk around Govardhan hill near Vrindavan.

games.q: it's Govardhan Puja at the temple, and there's a huge heap of food in front of Krishna's image. what is it?
o: an Annakut: a hill of food offered to Krishna, the way the village fed Govardhan.
a feast only the priests can eat.
games.why: the village cooked for the hill instead of Indra, and Krishna said, I am the hill. the food is shared with everyone afterward.

practice: At the end of a puja, many Hindus turn slowly in place, clockwise, a small circling like the cowherds walking around their hill. Stand, if you can, and turn once, slowly.

With each quarter turn, name something near that holds your life up: the ground under you, the water in your tap, the people who grew your food, the people who cook it. If you pray, give thanks to God in each of them.
If you don't, let gratitude rest on each one.

wordCard.voice: Govardhan lifted. It starts here: a boy asks why, and the village turns its offering toward the hill that shelters it.

carryVoice: Your line: God is in the hill that feeds you. Tomorrow, Indra answers with a storm. See you tomorrow.
